He taught high school math for thirty-one years. Same classroom. Same desk. Different kids every September. When he retired last spring, the school held a small ceremony in the gymnasium. Former students flew in from three states. One of them -- now a structural engineer -- told the crowd that Mr. Davis was the reason she passed calculus. Another -- a nurse -- said he was the first adult who ever told her she was smart. He stood at the podium and said almost nothing. He thanked his wife. He thanked the janitor who kept his room clean for three decades. He did not talk about test scores or graduation rates. He talked about showing up. Every day. Even the hard days. Especially the hard days. Teaching does not pay well. Everyone knows that. What people forget is what it costs -- emotionally, physically, personally. He gave the job everything. The job gave him a plaque and a handshake.
